title: Lamrim: calm and insight
hookLine: calm abiding and special insight into emptiness

lines: THE WIND DROPS. THE WATER CLEARS.
cards: A pond on a windy afternoon. The surface is all chop and glitter, and whatever lies on the bottom, a stone, a lost key, a fish, can't be seen. The wind drops.
The ripples flatten. Slowly the water turns clear, and there it all is. But a clear pond isn't the same as looking into it.
Someone still has to lean over and see what's down there. The Tibetan stages of the path end with exactly this pair: first let the water go still, then look.

teach.h: CALM: SHAMATHA, RESTING ON ONE THING.
teach.b: You met these two wings on day two hundred ninety-five; here they crown the staircase. First, calm. In Sanskrit, shamatha; Tibetans say shiné, calm abiding.
It's the training of resting the mind on one thing, the breath, an image of the Buddha, and staying, without drifting and without going dull.
Tibetan teachers describe it in stages, a wild mind slowly tamed, like an elephant learning to walk beside its keeper. Second, insight.
In Sanskrit, vipashyana; in Tibetan, lhaktong, special insight. Here the steady mind turns and looks: at the self, at things, at how they actually exist.
What it's meant to see, in this tradition, is emptiness: that nothing stands on its own the way it seems to, apart from causes and parts and the mind that names it. Third, why in that order.

teach.h: A STEADY FLAME, THEN READING BY IT.
teach.b: Insight without calm is like reading by a candle in a version: the flame jumps and you lose your place.

teach.h: A WEEK OF STAGES, CALM THEN INSIGHT.
teach.b: Calm without insight is a still pond nobody looks into, pleasant, but nothing changes underneath.

The Pali discourses already pair the two: a discourse in the Anguttara Nikaya names calm and insight as two things that lead toward true knowing. Fourth, where the week has led. A precious human life.
Death, certain, its time uncertain. Karma, small growing large. The round of suffering.
And now calm, then insight, the two wings the student flies on at the end of the road, the way Atisha and Tsongkhapa set it down.

how: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners train in calm abiding by resting the mind on a single object, then use that steadiness for analytical meditation on emptiness; the lamrim presents the union of the two as the culmination of the path.

o: the last stair: calm abiding joined with special insight
the last stair: memorizing the whole path by heart
the last stair: a calm so deep that nothing is seen

games.q: calm and insight: tap the pairs.
p: calm abiding, resting on one thing
a still pond nobody looks into

s: calm abiding is the whole goal of the lamrim
calm is the ground. insight, seeing how things exist, is what changes things underneath.
the Pali discourses already pair calm and insight
a discourse in the Anguttara Nikaya names them together as two things that lead toward true knowing.
in this tradition, insight looks toward emptiness
seeing that nothing stands on its own, apart from causes, parts and naming.

games.q: after weeks of practice, your mind finally goes still, like a pond with no wind. what does the lamrim say comes next?
o: stay there and call it done.
use the stillness to look closely at how things exist.
games.why: calm is the ground, not the goal. the lamrim ends with calm and insight joined: a still mind that looks.

practice: For the first part of the sit, rest your attention on the breath at the nostrils, and when the mind wanders, bring it back without scolding, letting it settle like the pond.
Then keep that stillness and turn to look: who is breathing? Where, exactly, is that person? Don't answer with words; just look, and see what you find, and what you don't.

wordCard.voice: Lamrim. The stages of the path. Its last stage: calm abiding and special insight, joined. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit vipashyana, special insight (Pali vipassana); its partner is shamatha (शमथ), calm.

carryVoice: Your line: calm, then insight. Still the water, then look. Seven stairs climbed, and a rest well earned.
